strengths: The paper addresses a relevant vulnerability in model auditing. Manipulating activation-maximization outputs through weight fine-tuning, without inserting additional circuits, is a meaningful extension of the architectural attacks discussed in prior work.

The gradient-matching objective and activation-preservation loss are understandable and well motivated. The quadratic construction and toy example provide useful intuition for redirecting optimization toward a chosen image.

The experiments demonstrate recognizable targeted manipulations in both pixel and Fourier domains. Quantitative similarity metrics, preservation–manipulation trade-offs, and a grid of 16 model configurations provide evidence beyond selected visual examples.

The appendix supplies substantial implementation detail and links a PyTorch implementation. The authors acknowledge computational limitations and unsuccessful defenses candidly. The benchmark study presents no evident material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The central claim of preserving model behavior with little performance degradation is overstated. In the main CIFAR-10 example, accuracy falls from 86.33% to 82.39% (Table 2), while cat AUROC falls from 0.970 to 0.938 (Figure 1). Figure 5 reports accuracy losses of 3.53–7.13 percentage points even for the widest models, with substantially larger losses for narrower models. Aggregate accuracy and one-class AUROC also do not establish preservation of individual predictions or internal representations.

The evaluation does not substantiate the stronger claim of concealing problematic or malicious representations during audits. Image experiments target the digit-zero output on MNIST and the cat output on CIFAR-10, using three chosen target images. There are no hidden-neuron experiments, actual backdoors or spurious-feature detectors, or evaluations of audit evasion while preserving the problematic behavior.

Attack generality and defensive effectiveness remain insufficiently established. The main attack assumes a known initialization distribution and fixed gradient-ascent settings, initially excluding transformation robustness. Defenses are evaluated on one selected manipulated model per dataset, without adaptive attacks. Transformation robustness restores the CIFAR-10 concept in one setting, whereas none of the tested strategies restores the MNIST concept. These are useful exploratory observations, but they do not establish a dependable remedy.

The contribution is distinguished from prior attacks primarily through a qualitative architectural argument. There are no empirical attack baselines or ablations isolating the benefits of the slingshot and landing zones. Comparisons at matched accuracy loss would help establish whether the proposed construction offers a favorable manipulation–preservation trade-off.

The theoretical support needs qualification. Equation (7) specifies an ideal piecewise function without establishing its realization by the unchanged network or connecting the sampled gradient loss to a uniform approximation guarantee. Appendix A's noisy-gradient argument supplies a sufficient first-step landing bound; its description as a necessary/minimax result is not justified by the loose bound used. It also does not establish convergence to the target under nonzero gradient error.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting have remaining gaps despite the linked implementation. Training is specified as continuing 'until convergence' without a precise stopping rule, and independent training/fine-tuning repetitions are not reported. Some instructions cannot be followed literally: Appendix B samples from the intersection of two disjoint balls, and Appendix C specifies a negative lower bound for Torchvision's affine scale. These inconsistencies require correction.
